newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Andreotti faces chief accuser in court.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Andreotti faces chief accuser in court.

text.p: Italy's former prime minister Giulio Andreotti came face-to-face in court on Monday with the Mafia turncoat central to the prosecution case at his trial for alleged complicity in murder.

The encounter between Andreotti, prime minister seven times, and former Mafia boss Tommaso Buscetta took place amid a heavy police presence at a high security courtroom attached to a prison in Perugia, central Italy, where the trial is under way.
Buscetta, the first leading Mafioso to turn state's evidence, was expected to testify for up to two days.
Interest in his appearance has surged amid a debate on the reliability of turncoats, whose evidence has contributed to a string of arrests of key Mafiosi since 1993.

The debate follows recent evidence that one informer organised killings while under police protection and suspicion that a decision by arrested godfather Giovanni Brusca to cooperate with investigators may be a ploy to disrupt inquiries.
Buscetta's testimony was carried live on Italian radio.

He said he had not revealed what he knew of links between the Mafia and politics until the recent demise of Andreotti's Christian Democrats in Italy's corruption scandals "because it wasn't my impression that the state wanted to fight organised crime".

He repeated his allegation that mobsters shot dead a muck-raking journalist, Mino Pecorelli, in 1979 as a favour to Andreotti to halt exposure of damaging details about the leftist guerrilla kidnapping and murder of former premier Aldo Moro.
Andreotti, who is also being tried separately in the Sicilian capital Palermo on charges of collusion with the Mafia, heard Buscetta testify against him in that case last January.

The 77-year-old life senator, a symbol of the political order the Christian Democrats led for almost 50 years, has denied any links to the Mafia, which he says is seeking revenge for crackdowns on crime during his years in government.
He was visibly shaken by the crush of journalists at the court but said he had nothing to fear from Buscetta.
Asked what he expected to emerge from Buscetta's testimony, he said: "Nothing. I heard him for two days (in January) so I know pretty well what he has to say".
Buscetta, who became the first leading Mafioso to turn state's evidence in the 1980s, lives mainly in the United States under heavy protection.

He had grown a moustache since his last published photograph a year ago and wore a beige suit for his court appearance. He told judges he would dispense with a screen set up in the courtoom to conceal his identity.
Buscetta has alleged that the killing of Pecorelli, who published a political gossip magazine, was organised by Mafia godfathers as a "personal favour" to Andreotti.

The Mafioso Buscetta cited as the source of the information, Gaetano Badalamenti, has denied discussing the affair with him and refused to come to Italy to testify from the United States, where he is serving a lengthy jail term.

Badalamenti is one of four co-defendants with Andreotti at the Pecorelli trial. Three of the other accused, former foreign trade minister Claudio Vitalone and mobsters Pippo Calo and Massimo Carminati, were present in court on Monday.
